[MUQATIL:55:1-4/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | When Meccan polytheists were told to prostrate to al-Rahman, they denied knowing that name; God identifies Himself and recounts His works so people may know and worship Him alone. | mentions 25:60
[ZAJJAJ:v5p95/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Al-Raḥmān is a name exclusive to God, found in earlier scriptures, meaning abundant in mercy.
[NAHHAS:v4p303/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | الرحمن begins as a nominative subject, with its predicate supplied in the following construction.
[SULAMI:v2p292#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | They compare God's teaching all names to angels with His teaching Muhammad the Qur'an, which He presents to Himself; the disputing high assembly means the angels.
[THALABI:v9p177#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | One reported occasion for the opening is that people asked, “What is the All-Merciful?”
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p422#2/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن وقطرب | reports | They say الرحمن is a divine name people cannot appropriate for themselves.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p422#2/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · سعيد بن جبير وابن عباس | reports | They combine the initials الر, حم, and ن from three surahs to form one of God's names, الرحمن.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p262/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The basmala announces God's might and greatness as well as His bounty and mercy; witnessing majesty completes the spirits' joy and experiencing mercy brings bodily bliss, for majesty makes Him worshiped and mercy makes Him loved.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p133#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | When 17:110 was revealed, Meccan disbelievers said they knew only Musaylima, the Rahman of al-Yamama; 25:60 records their denial of the name. | mentions 17:110, 25:60
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p133#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | God identifies himself by mentioning his works so that people will recognize him and affirm his oneness.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p438#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | One report says the opening name al-Raḥmān was revealed when people asked who the Merciful was.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p438#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Another report takes al-Raḥmān as an answer to Meccans who claimed a human taught the Prophet.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p442/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Zamakhsharī places the Quran first among divine favors because religion is the foremost favor; its revelation and teaching are the highest-ranked revelation and the summit, proof, and standard of heavenly books.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p442/r10] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The first clauses omit conjunctions so each independently rebukes deniers by enumerating benefactions; conjunctions resume for clauses that suit and approach each other.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p442/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Mentioning human creation after the Quran shows that humanity was created for religion and to know revelation and scripture; the purpose of human creation is presented as prior to creation.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p442/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Al-Raḥmān is the subject; the following verbs with their pronouns form successive predicates without conjunctions, matching a listing of favors and making each clause an independent rebuke to deniers.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p442/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | He illustrates the rebuke by listing how Zayd was helped after poverty, lowliness, and scarcity, then asking what kindness he could deny.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p223#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Raḥmān is an intensive form derived from mercy and a name whose attribute belongs uniquely to God.
[TABRISI:55:1-13/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | When told to call upon God or the Merciful, Meccans denied knowing the latter name; revelation clarifies who al-Raḥmān is. | mentions 17:110
[TABRISI:55:1-13/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-Raḥmān denotes the One whose mercy encompasses everything and is reserved for God; raḥim and raḥīm may also describe people.
[TABRISI:55:1-13/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-Raḥmān is elliptical for “God, the Merciful,” so it can stand as a verse and preserve the verse-ending pattern.
[TABRISI:55:1-13/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The name answers Meccans who asked who the Merciful was after being told to worship Him. | mentions 25:60
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p105/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مقاتل | reports | When Meccan unbelievers rejected the name al-Rahman after 25:60 was revealed, God identified the rejected al-Rahman as the one who taught the Quran. | mentions 25:60
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | Some treat Allah, and some also al-Rahman, as proper names; they cite the permission to invoke either name and allow the vocative ‘O All-Merciful.’ | mentions 17:110
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi rejects those proper-name claims as weak, especially the vocative ‘O All-Merciful.’ | mentions 17:110
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Allah is unlikely to be a proper name with the article because its initial hamza would then be radical and could not drop as a hamzat waṣl in forms such as ‘creation of Allah.’
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A sound alternative makes Ilāh or Lāh the proper name for the creator, with the article later attached as in other personal names.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On the proper-name analysis, God’s sovereign reservation of a name makes idolaters’ naming idols with it transgressive, even if language alone permits the usage.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, Ilāh or Lāh means ‘the one worshipped’; because that meaning belongs only to God, the definite name cannot be given to another, even a son, lest it imply the meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Names such as al-Karim and al-Wadud are permissible because their meanings may also be intended, whereas al-Khaliq, al-Qadim, and ‘the worshipped’ cannot be given to people.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Given this analysis of Allah, treating al-Rahman as a proper name is even less defensible, and permitting ‘O All-Merciful’ is weakest of all.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The opening contrasts the prior surah’s display of majesty through the moon’s splitting with this surah’s merciful miracle, the Qur’an that purifies hearts of sins. | mentions 54:1
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The prior surah repeatedly recalls punishment, while this surah repeatedly recalls divine favors, matching their respective emphasis on awe and mercy. | mentions 54:16
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The repeated refrain about divine favors completes the contrast with the prior surah’s repeated warning about punishment. | mentions 55:13
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The ending of al-Qamar, ‘with a Sovereign, Powerful,’ leads into al-Rahman: power signals majesty, while this opening gathers divine might toward disbelievers and mercy toward the righteous. | mentions 54:55
[RAZI-FULL:v29p73/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | ‘The All-Merciful’ describes God as mighty, avenging, and powerful toward disbelievers and wicked people, but as merciful, beneficent, and forgiving toward the righteous.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rahman functions like an original name paired with a dominant epithet that became name-like through frequent use, but it is exclusive to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Calling the Yamami man al-Rahman is a linguistic possibility used transgressively, like calling another being ‘a god,’ and rests on false belief.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God has prior mercy in creating beings and later mercy in sustaining them with provision, understanding, and aid; hence He is al-Rahman for the first and al-Rahim for the latter.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | No one else may be called al-Rahman because no other being creates; people may be called rahim insofar as they imitate later mercy by feeding, clothing, and helping others.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Grammatically, al-Rahman is the subject whose predicate is the verbal sentence ‘He taught the Qur’an’; this is the sounder analysis.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A weaker parse makes al-Rahman the predicate of an omitted ‘He is,’ and treats it as a standalone verse.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p74/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Razi prefers the first grammatical analysis; the second depends on the weaker standalone-verse reading.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If Qur’an teaching means teaching angels, God taught them before creating humans; the preserved Qur’an is touched only by the purified and then sent down from the Lord of the worlds. | mentions 56:77, 56:78, 56:79, 56:80
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | This order pairs celestial matters with earthly ones and names the celestial first: Qur’an teaching above is paired with teaching expression to humans below.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The sun and moon among celestial signs are paired with the stars and trees prostrating among earthly signs. | mentions 75:9, 55:6
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The raised heaven is paired with the placed earth, continuing the sequence of celestial signs before earthly ones. | mentions 55:7, 55:10
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, Qur’an teaching comes first because it is the greatest favor; ‘created humanity, taugh

[RAZI-FULL:v29p75/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively, God made the Qur’an learnable, as in ‘We made the Qur’an easy for remembrance’; teaching here is metaphorical, as when one funds a learner’s instruction. | mentions 54:17
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The omitted second object may be Gabriel and other angels: God taught them the Qur’an and then sent it down to His servant. | mentions 26:193, 26:194

[RAZI-FULL:v29p75/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Teaching means imparting knowledge; the statement does not conflict with 3:7, whether the learned are joined to God or treated as a separate clause that can learn difficult passages within human capacity. | mentions 3:7
[RAZI-FULL:v29p75/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On a reading that stops at ‘except God,’ no one independently discovers the Qur’an’s interpretation through intellect; people know only what God teaches them. | mentions 3:7
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:1-5/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbī take the opening as the combined initials alif-lām-rāʾ, ḥā-mīm, and nūn, forming one of God’s names, al-Raḥmān.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:55:1-4/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Because the sūrah enumerates worldly and otherworldly blessings, it opens with the name al-Raḥmān.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p199#7/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The word al-insan in the creation verse may mean humanity as a kind, Adam, or Muhammad.
[QASHANI:55:1-2/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | “The All-Merciful” names God as the giver, at the beginning, of all foundational blessings: entities and their first perfections; its broad scope grounds the attributes that follow.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p53/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Most say the surah is Meccan; Ibn Masʿud says Medinan. Ibn Abbas reports both and says verse 29 is a Medinan exception in one account. | mentions 55:29
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p53/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مقاتل | reports | He says the surah followed people's refusal to prostrate to الرحمن because they did not know the name, prompting الرحمن علم القرآن. | mentions 25:60
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p53/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another view says it was revealed in Medina when Suhayl ibn ʿAmr and others refused to write the basmala in the treaty.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p53/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | After the preceding surah briefly names the righteous' abode with the mighty King, this surah details divine signs and expands both groups' destinations. | mentions 54:55
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p54/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Teaching the Qur'an is an effect of mercy and heals hearts; الرحمن is apparently the subject and علم القرآن its predicate, though another parse supplies an omitted predicate.
[SAMIN-DURR:55:1/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | For those counting al-Rahman as a verse together with an implied element, it can be the predicate of an unspoken subject: “God is al-Rahman.”
[SAMIN-DURR:55:1/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, for the same verse-counting view, al-Rahman can be the subject with an omitted predicate: “Al-Rahman is our Lord.”
[SAMIN-DURR:55:1/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A third analysis does not count al-Rahman as a verse by itself; it begins one clause with what follows, with “taught the Quran” as its predicate. | mentions 55:2

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p488/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud says the Prophet paired the opening surahs of the Mufassal two by two; in his arrangement, al-Rahman began the Mufassal.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p488/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جابر | reports | Jabir reports that the Prophet recited all of al-Rahman to his companions; they were silent, and the Prophet recalled the jinn's better response to its repeated refrain.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p488/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الترمذي | reports | Al-Tirmidhi calls the Jabir report gharīb, known only through al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p488/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · البزار | reports | Al-Bazzar says the Jabir narration is known only by this route through al-Walid ibn Muslim.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p488/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar reports that the Prophet read al-Rahman, or it was read in his presence, and remarked on the jinn's better response.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p488/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · البزار | reports | Al-Bazzar says the Ibn Umar hadith is known from the Prophet only through this chain.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p489#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God's favor and mercy include sending the Quran to His servants and making its memorization and understanding easy for those He shows mercy.
[BURHAN:v1p245/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن السيد | reports | Ibn al-Sayyid says the ninth division begins with al-Raḥmān and attributes that arrangement to Ibn Masʿūd's codex; al-Zarkashī says Aḥmad likewise transmits it.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p370#s055/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The surah’s purpose is to establish God’s universal mercy, inviting hope in His gifts and warning that He may end further favor through punishment; it does so by recounting creation’s wonders and blessings.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p370#s055/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The title ‘Bride of the Qur’an’ evokes its gathering of adornments, garments, jewels, crowns, blessings, beauty, and perfection.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p370#s055/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The basmala describes God’s perfection as shown in creation, universal mercy in wondrous works and signs, and special mercy to the obedient through worship.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p371/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After the preceding surah’s emphasis on sovereignty and power, this surah counts blessings in both worlds; universal mercy completes kingship, and its opening name signals that theme.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p371/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · ابن برجان | reports | Ibn Burjān describes the name al-Raḥmān as the manifest aspect of the name Allah and the hidden aspect of the name al-Rabb; the three names disclose and veil the divine essence to creatures.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p372/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Qur'an is the greatest blessing, the summit and foundation of the heavenly books, clarifying what pleases God and what must be avoided; it leads to the promised abode. | mentions 2:31
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p372/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · جعفر بن الزبير | reports | Jaʿfar says the whole Qur'an is miraculous and its arrangement overpowers opponents, while some passages disclose its eloquence more immediately; he points to Sūrat al-Qamar's concise stories that still complete their aims and admonitions. | mentions 11:44, 15:94, 54:17, 54:18
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p372/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The commentary gives the address to earth and sky and the command to proclaim as examples of instantly evident Qur'anic eloquence. | mentions 11:44, 15:94
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p372/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The name al-Raḥmān signals God's mercy and immense beneficence through the Qur'an, whose blessings cannot be enumerated. | mentions 14:34
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p372/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Sūrat al-Raḥmān follows al-Qamar to address both humans and jinn, establish proof for both kinds, and repeatedly remind them of God's favors.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p399/r20] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الرازي | reports | Al-Rāzī says the closing Name refers back to the opening Name of the sūrah, encompassing both Qur'anic teaching and divine punishment.
[ITQAN:v1p43/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | prefers | Suyūṭī holds that the majority correctly classify al-Raḥmān as Meccan; al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim report that the jinn responded to the refrain more warmly than the Companions, and al-Ḥākim grades the report sound on the two Shaykhs’ condition. | mentions 15:87
[ITQAN:v1p43/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · أسماء بنت أبي بكر | reports | A good-chain report from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr says she heard the Prophet reciting al-Raḥmān near the Kaʿba corner before public proclamation while the polytheists listened; this more clearly shows it preceded al-Ḥijr.
[BURSEVI:v9p235#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | The surah is called the Bride of the Quran; the source gives differing reports about whether it is Meccan or Medinan and about its verse count.
[BURSEVI:v9p235#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | “The All-Merciful” begins the sentence and means the One whose mercy is complete; worldly provision is general, while forgiveness in the afterlife is granted to believers.
